text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes explain references in Harbarthsljoth to Valland, the bringing of slain heroes to Othin, Thor's encounter with the giant Skrymir and his glove-shaped shelter, the river Ifing and the giants who defend its passage, Othin's use of magic to seek information from the dead, berserkers associated with bear transformation, Thor's kin and place names, and textual or speaker-attribution variants.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Valland is described as a mythical place whose name means Land of Slaughter; it is not further characterized in the notes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes refer to slain heroes being brought to Othin and state that Thor is otherwise not shown as having an asylum for dead peasants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Thor and his companions enter a house in a forest to spend the night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An earthquake and a terrific noise disturb Thor and his companions, who crawl into a smaller room opening from the main room.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The next morning, the house is identified as the glove of the giant Skrymir, and the smaller room as the thumb; the earthquake resulted from Skrymir lying down nearby and the noise from his snoring.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The river is probably Ifing, described as lying between the land of the gods and the land of the giants; the sons of Svarang are presumed to be giants defending the passage.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"An editorial note records a variant concerning Othin's encounter with an unnamed woman: one reading has an encounter by stealth and another has a long meeting with her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The term Heel-biter is identified as an unusual parallel to back-biter in Old Norse.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The women associated with berserkers are described as belonging to an earlier type in which people could turn themselves into bears.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Thjalfi is identified as Thor's servant.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Othin speaks of an expedition whose destination or purpose is unknown and may describe himself as allied with the foes of the gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A textual variant gives either hatred or sickness for a term in the passage.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The meaning of Othin's words in another passage is uncertain; the note suggests that he may imply Thor is open to bribery, and that preceding material may be missing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Othin is said to refer to the dead, from whom he seeks information through magic power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Sif is identified as Thor's wife, and Loki is presented as the presumed lover in the referenced passage.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Asathor is explained as meaning Thor of the Gods; Thor has several other names in the poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Magni is identified as Thor's son.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Verland is described as the Land of Men, which Thor must reach from the land of the giants; Fjorgyn is interpreted here as Jorth or Earth, Thor's mother, and the road as the rainbow bridge Bifrost.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A manuscript variant changes a phrase concerning the time before sunrise.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The final note assigns a line to Harbarth in one manuscript tradition, while another manuscript lacks a superscription and may assign it to Thor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Valland","description":"A mythical place whose name is glossed as Land of Othin.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"A figure associated with receiving slain heroes, seeking information from the dead through The notes explain nautical terms and places, identify speakers and figures, discuss a dialogue involving Gothmund and Sinfjotli, describe werewolf and mare transformations, and record editorial uncertainties and parallels with related texts.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The high, curving stem of a Norse ship is described as long-headed and often carved to represent a head and neck.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ships-tents are identified as awnings spread over a ship's deck to shelter crews from sun and rain while anchored.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The waves are called the Sisters of Kolga; Kolga is identified as one of the maritime episode.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sigrun appears again as a Valkyrie; a sea-beast is identified as a ship, and Gnipalund is translated as Crag-Wood.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Unavagar is translated as Friendly Waves, and Svarins hill is identified as the hill where Granmar had his dwelling.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A long dialogue begins between Gothmund, one of Granmar's sons, and Sinfjotli, Helgi's half-brother.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes report that the dialogue is closely paralleled in stanzas 22–27 of the second Helgi Hundingsbane lay and discuss possible interpolation or use of an older poem.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Raising a red shield is identified as a signal for war.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Volsungasaga is said to describe Sigmund and Sinfjotli living in the woods for a time as werewolves.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes state that reproaching a man with having been a woman and having borne children was not uncommon.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The phrase Allfather is identified with Othin, while the notes say that Gothmund's career is unknown and that Sinfjotli may be drawing on imagination in some taunts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Fenrirs-wolves is explained as referring to wolves in general; Thorsnes is translated as Thors Cape.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The notes say Gothmund may mean that Sinfjotli had turned into a mare, after the fashion of Loki; Grani is identified as Sigurth's horse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15","ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Moinsheimar is identified as an otherwise unknown battlefield where the sons of Granmar The birds warn Sigurth that Regin intends betrayal.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Fafnir says that some person will hold the hoard until a destined day, after which every person will journey to hell.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fafnir describes the Norns as beings of many births, related variously to gods, elves, and Dvalin's daughters; Sigurth asks which Norns bring the infant from the mother.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fafnir names Oskopnir as an island where the gods and Surt will mingle in sword battle; he says Bifrost will break and the steeds will swim in a flood.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fafnir says he used a fear-helm to frighten mankind while guarding his gold and that he breathed venom while lying beside the hoard.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Fafnir warns Sigurth that the gold, red wealth, and rings will be his bane, and says that Regin betrayed Fafnir and will betray Sigurth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Regin returns after the fight and claims that his forged weapon contributed to Fafnir's death; Sigurth answers that Regin hid while Sigurth fought the dragon.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Regin cuts out Fafnir's heart and drinks blood from the wounds. Sigurth cooks the heart, burns his finger while testing it, puts the finger in his mouth, and then understands the speech of birds when the heart's blood reaches his tongue.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Nut-hatches or birds say that Regin plans to betray Sigurth and advise Sigurth about Regin, the wealth, and the fact that Regin is the brother of the slain Fafnir.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Sigurth states that courage and a person's heart matter more in battle than the strength / THE BALLAD OF FAFNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 15126-15171","start":"15126","end":"15171","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss two possible bird speeches representing different versions of Sigurth's destination, identify figures and kennings associated with Brynhild, and explain the editorial history of the name Sigrdrifa and the prose transition to Sigrdrifumol.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note states that the manuscript and editions do not clearly indicate more than one bird in stanzas 40–44, while proposing that there may be two birds and two distinct stories.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Stanzas 40–41 are described as applying to Guthrun and as indicating that Sigurth will go directly to Gunnar's hall.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Stanzas 42–44 are described as applying to Brynhild and as indicating that Sigurth will find her before visiting the Gjukungs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The note attributes the confusion between the two versions to a difference in the final working out of Brynhild's revenge.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The note says that two birds might be speaking, each reflecting one version, or that one speech might have been added later or taken from another poem.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Volsungasaga is said to condense the passage into one bird's words: Sigurth should ride to Hindarfjoll, where Brynhild sleeps and where he would gain much wisdom; the Guthrun-bird is absent there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gjuki is identified as the father of Gunnar and Guthrun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hindarfjoll is glossed as Mountain of the Hind, and 'Light of the flood' is glossed as gold.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild is identified as a battle-maid and Valkyrie; 'bane of the wood' is glossed as fire; Ygg is identified with Othin; and the thorn is identified as a sleep-thorn.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Vingskornir is identified as Brynhild's horse, and sigrdrifa is explained as an epithet meaning Victory-bringer rather than a separate Valkyrie's proper name.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The note says that the manuscript has no break between the prose passage and the prose introducing Sigrdrifumol, leaving editors to assign the passage differently.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Guthrun-bird","description":"A bird associated in the note with the version in which Sigurth goes directly to Gunnar's hall; it is absent from the Volsungasaga version described.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Possible second bird","description":"A possible second bird said to reflect the Brynhild version of the story; the note does not give it a personal name.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"The figure whose destination differs between the two versions and who is said to ride to Hindarfjoll in the Volsungasaga summary.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"The figure to whom stanzas 40–41 are said to apply.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"The figure whose hall Sigurth is said to reach in one version; he is identified as Guthrun's brother and Gjuki's son in the note.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Brynhild","description":"A battle-maid and Valkyrie who sleeps at Hindarfjoll in the reported Volsungasaga version; she is also associated with the horse Vingskornir.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Gjukungs","description":"The group whom Sigurth visits after finding Brynhild in the version described in the note.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Gjuki","description":"The father of Gunnar and Guthrun.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Vingskornir","description":"Brynhild's horse, according to the She identifies herself as the Valkyrie Sigrdrifa, explains that Othin punished her with enchanted sleep after a battle, and gives Sigurth a memory-draught. She then teaches him multiple kinds of runes, their uses and places of inscription, and describes their origin and distribution among gods, elves, Wanes, and mortals. The passage ends with a speaker identified as Brynhild offering Sigurth a choice between speech and silence.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigurth rides up on Hindarfjoll and turns southward toward the land of the Franks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"On the mountain, Sigurth sees a great light compared to burning fire, with a glow reaching toward heaven.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A tower of shields with a banner stands at the site, and a person lies sleeping inside wearing war-weapons and a mail-coat memory-draught.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The woman says that she is Sigrdrifa, a Valkyrie, and recounts that she slew Hjalmgunnar after Othin had promised him victory; Othin punished her with a sleep-thorn and decreed that she would thereafter be wedded.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Sigrdrifa says that she had vowed not to marry a man who knew the meaning of fear, and Sigurth asks her to teach him wisdom concerning what takes place in all the thought.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The verses direct that runes be written or cut on swords, horns, hands, nails, ships, oars, bark, trees, and other listed content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15442-l15532","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / SIGRDRIFUMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE VICTORY-BRINGER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 15442-15532","start":"15442","end":"15532","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Then first I rede thee, that free of guilt / Toward kinsmen ever thou art.","summary":"Stanzas 21–37 present an opening statement followed by ten numbered counsels. The speaker advises the addressee about kinship, oaths, public speech, witches, sexual conduct, drunken conflict, battle, burial of the dead, distrust of enemies, and treachery.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The first-person speaker says that it will not flee even though its fate is near and says it was not born a coward.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker advises the addressee to remain free of guilt toward kinsmen, avoid vengeance even when harmed, and says that a reward will follow after death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker advises against swearing an oath when its truth is not known and warns of the fate of an oath-breaker.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker advises the addressee not to argue in words with fools at the Thing, warns that silence may be called cowardice, and connects fame with later punishment for lies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker advises leaving rather than becoming the guest of a wily witch and says that evil witches may sit by the way and blunt blade and courage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker warns against allowing maidens, women's kisses, or sexual desire to disturb judgment, and advises avoiding words with a drunken warrior during an ale-fueled quarrel.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker says that, when facing a powerful foe, it is better to fight than to burn alive in the hall of a wealthy hero.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker instructs the addressee to bury a fallen corpse, wash the body, wipe and comb it, place it in a coffin, and pray that it sleeps in peace.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker warns against trusting the race of wolves, including a son who may contain a wolf despite accepting gold, and says that battle, hatred, and harm seldom sleep.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker advises the addressee to shun wrath and false Sorli.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A paraphrase of Volsungasaga describes Erp's death, Hamther's stumble and recovery by using his hand, a similar incident involving Sorli, and the brothers' realization that they had wronged Erp.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hamther and Sorli are said to be killed by stoning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Randver is identified as Jormunrek's son, hanged by his father on Bikki's advice.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The phrase 'ill way' is interpreted as possibly referring to the road through the gate of Jormunrek's town where dead.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The phrase 'scather of twigs' is explained as a poetic circumlocution for the wind, although some editors interpret it content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1153-l1260","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1153-1260","start":"1153","end":"1260","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A princess hosts the stranger Jemshd at a fountain, recognizes him through his manner, archery skill, lineage, and resemblance to a portrait, and accepts a marriage wager. Her nurse confirms through horoscope signs that he is destined to be her spouse and that they will have a conquering son. Jemshd recognizes his former royal identity in the portrait and weeps over his lost throne and diadem.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The princess and Jemshd arrive at a fountain, sit on royal carpets facing each other, and receive music, wine, and refreshments.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The princess's handmaids wash the stranger's feet and sit attentively near the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Jemshd drinks three cups of ruby wine, after which the narration says that sorrow and signs of past affliction leave his heart and face.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The princess infers from Jemshd's manner and eloquence that he is a king and considers comparing him with a portrait of Jemshd in her father's gallery.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Jemshd describes wine as removing thoughts of enemies and sorrow and as giving wisdom, joy, courage, youth, vigor, and color.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A male and female pair of ring-doves land near the fountain and engage in amorous billing and cooing.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The princess asks Jemshd to identify which dove she should shoot, and he responds that he should use the bow himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The princess turns aside in shame, gives Jemshd the bow, and the narration states that her heart is full of love.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Jemshd wagers that if he hits the female dove, the lady he most admires will be his; the princess assents.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Jemshd shoots the female dove through both wings; the male dove flies away, then returns to the same place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The princess makes a reciprocal wager that if her aim succeeds, the man she chooses will be her husband.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Kbul nurse examines Jemshd, recognizes him, and says that the horoscope's predictions are being fulfilled.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The nurse says that God has brought Jemshd to be the princess's spouse and will bless them with a son who will conquer the world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The princess had become enamored of the stranger before learning his identity, and the nurse's identification increases her affection.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The princess receives a portrait of Jemshd, finds the resemblance exact, and gives it to him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Jemshd recognizes his own likeness in the portrait, remembers the diadem and throne he no longer possesses, and weeps in anguish.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Jemshd is identified as the son of Tahmers, who is called the Binder of Demons.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Jemshd","description":"A stranger identified as King Jemshd, son of Tahmers; he drinks wine, uses the bow, accepts a marriage wager, and remembers his former throne.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5","ev:8","ev:9","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"The young princess","description":"A princess who hosts Jemshd, tests his identity through observation and archery, and chooses him as a prospective husband.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"The handmaids","description":"The princess's attendants who wash the Rustem escorts Kai-kobd to Persia, defeats pursuing enemies, and witnesses his coronation after seven days of council.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem rides Rakush with a powerful force toward Mount Alberz and overcomes troops and other obstacles on the road.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Near Alberz, Rustem sees a wooded and watered place where a young man sits on a throne among companions and after being told that he will receive information there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The young man takes Rustem's hand, gives him wine, asks who sent him, and The king rejects an offer to submit, leading to an eight-day battle. During combat, the king uses magic to transform into a rock, but Rustem moves and threatens the rock until the king resumes his original form. Ks orders the king executed, appoints Ald governor, and returns to Persia with his warriors; Rustem returns to his father Zl. Ks later tours his empire, suppresses a rebellion in Berberistan, visits Mount Kaf and other lands, and stays for a month with the son of Zl in Zbulistan.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem approaches the court of the king of Mzindern while the hostile army is in sight, and a deputation of warriors is sent to receive him.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rustem uproots a large tree, wields it like a spear, and throws it before the opposing warriors.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"An unnamed chief and then Klahr challenge Rustem by grasping his hand; Rustem injures both through the force of his grip.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem tells the king that he is only Ks's servant and praises Ks as an exceptionally powerful warrior.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The armies fight for seven days without a victor; Ks prays for triumph, and the battle resumes on the eighth day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"During combat with Rustem, the king of Mzindern uses magic to transform himself into a stony rock.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The soldiers cannot move the rock, but Rustem lifts and carries it; after Rustem threatens to break it, the king resumes his Gdarz persuades the king to relent, and the king sends the warriors to ask Rustem to return.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ts, Gdarz, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7647-l7764","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7647-7764","start":"7647","end":"7764","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Saiwush is captured after attempting to flee, imprisoned, and then executed on Afrsiyb's orders. His blood is collected, though some falls on the soil and produces a tree later called Saiwush. His body is buried by Plsam, while Ferangs mourns and is threatened with death because she may bear Saiwush's child. Prn intervenes and takes Ferangs into his household, subject to Afrsiyb's demand that the child be brought to him after birth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the Irnians and Saiwush's horse are killed, Saiwush attempts to continue on foot but is surrounded and captured.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Afrsiyb initially wants Saiwush shot, but his people intercede and recommend that Saiwush be taken alive and imprisoned.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Saiwush is fettered and taken to the royal residence and city that he had built and richly ornamented.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ferangs appeals to Afrsiyb for mercy, declaring Saiwush faithful to her and not responsible for the conflict with Gerswaz.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Afrsiyb confines Ferangs in a remote part of the palace after briefly feeling compunction.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Afrsiyb orders Gerswaz to have Saiwush beheaded and commands that Saiwush's blood not stain the earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gerswaz directs Kar-zra to execute Saiwush; Kar-zra throws Saiwush to the ground and severs his head from his body.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Before his death, Saiwush prays that a son may be born who will vindicate his name and take revenge on his murderer.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A golden vessel receives Saiwush's blood, but a few drops spill onto the soil.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A tree grows at the place where Saiwush's blood was spilled; it is later called Saiwush and believed to possess many virtues.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Plsam buries Saiwush's body with respect and affection, while Saiwush's head is fixed on a javelin and his blood is conveyed to Afrsiyb.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A tremendous tempest and total darkness are said to occur when Saiwush is murdered.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The people execrate Afrsiyb and preserve the memory of Saiwush.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After learning of Saiwush's death and Ferangs's grief, Afrsiyb orders Gerswaz to have Ferangs killed so that no child of her marriage with Saiwush will survive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Prn protests against killing Ferangs and her unborn child and offers to keep Ferangs in his own household.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Afrsiyb permits Ferangs to go to Prn's home but orders that the child be brought to him after Ts's attack on a fort causes the death of Ferd and Ferd's mother Glshaher; Ts later erects a scented monument for them. After several reversals, Kai-khosru condemns and imprisons Ts, while Frburz and other commanders continue the war. Gdarz's forces recover the imperial banner through Byzun and use it to rally their troops, though the Turanians ultimately win the battle. Ts is later released, and another extended battle ends undecided after single combat between Gw and Hmn.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ts attacks a fort and the gates are broken open.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ferd fights Byzun; Bhrm emerges from ambush and kills Ferd by striking him on the head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Glshaher embraces the dead Ferd, then plunges a dagger into her own breast and dies at his feet.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ts remains at the place for three days and erects a lofty monument to Ferd, scenting it with musk and camphor.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ts's forces continue attacking forts and advancing toward Afrsiyb; opposing forces include Nizd's thirty thousand horsemen and Prn-wsah's forty thousand horsemen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Prn-wsah's forces conduct a night attack while many Persians are intoxicated, causing heavy Persian losses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kai-khosru states that Ts disobeyed orders concerning the residence of his brother and mother, which he says ought to have been kept sacred; he orders Ts bound and sent to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Frburz confines Ts and sends him to Khosru, who reproaches him and places him in a dungeon.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Frburz is driven to extremity and shelters with his remaining troops on the skirts of a mountain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gdarz and Gw decide to hold their ground or perish and ask that the imperial banner be brought to them if Frburz cannot join them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Byzun kills the standard-bearer, takes the Derafsh Gvahn, and conveys it to Gdarz, who raises it and directs his troops against the enemy.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The battle causes extensive casualties among the families and forces of both sides, but victory remains with the Trnians.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Afrsiyb gives presents and honorary dresses to his officers and says that Rustem's and Khosru's martial glory must still be obscured.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Frburz returns by night to Khosru's court; Khosru grieves over the defeat and Ferd's death, and Rustem is consulted.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Khosru releases Ts and sends Ts and Gdarz with a large army against Prn.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The armies fight for seven days and nights; on the eighth day Hmn challenges warriors singly, kills several, and fights Gw after Gdarz prevents Ts from accepting the challenge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Gw and Hmn are wounded and exhausted, return to their respective posts, and the renewed battle remains undecided.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ts","description":"Persian commander who attacks the fort, is blamed for the deaths of Ferd and Glshaher, is imprisoned by Khosru, and later commands another army.","role_refs":["role:1","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ferd","description":"Young defender of the fort who is killed by Bhrm during combat with Byzun.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Bhrm","description":"Hero who emerges from ambush and kills Ferd.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Glshaher","description":"Mother of Ferd who grieves over his death and kills herself with a dagger.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Kai-khosru / Khosru","description":"Persian king who condemns Ts, imprisons him, receives Frburz after defeat, grieves over the losses, and later releases Ts.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Frburz","description":"Persian commander who assumes command after Ts's arrest, is driven to a mountain refuge, refuses to surrender the imperial banner, and later returns to Khosru's court.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Byzun","description":"Warrior who fights Ferd, is rescued in battle, and later takes the Derafsh Gvahn to Gdarz.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Afrsiyb","description":"Turanian ruler who orders forces against the Persians, celebrates the victory, and rewards his officers.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Prn-wsah / Prn","description":"Turanian commander who leads a force, uses He conceals warriors in chests carried by camels, gains access to King Arjsp, and uses false information to maintain his disguise. Within the fortress he discovers that his two sisters are forced to draw and carry water. They recognize him by his voice, and he reveals that he is working to restore their liberty while instructing them to continue their labor until an opportunity for action arises.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Isfendiyr reconnoiters the Brazen Fortress, becomes convinced that it cannot be taken by ordinary military means, and feels sorrow and despair.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A Fakr reports that the fortress contains one hundred thousand veteran warriors, abundant supplies, and streams of pure water.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After his officers recommend retreat, Isfendiyr refuses, invokes God's power, and decides to enter the fortress disguised as a merchant.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Isfendiyr places Bashtan temporarily in command of the army and arranges for a column of flame and smoke to signal an attack from outside the fortress.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The caravan consists of one hundred dromedaries carrying merchandise, concealed warriors, and attendants; one hundred sixty warriors are hidden in chests and one hundred others serve as camel-drivers and servants.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The caravan claims to be bringing valuable goods from Persia, and Arjsp permits it to enter the fortress.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Isfendiyr, using the name Kherd, presents gifts to Arjsp and is granted access to the royal palace.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When Arjsp questions him about events in Persia, Isfendiyr gives a false account of his departure and of Isfendiyr's intended route through the Heft-khan.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Isfendiyr discovers that his two sisters are forced to draw and carry water for Arjsp's kitchen.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The sisters ask about their father and brother, while Isfendiyr hides his identity and tells them that he knows nothing about them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The elder sister recognizes Isfendiyr by his voice; the sisters keep the discovery secret until night and return to speak with him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Isfendiyr acknowledges his identity, says that he has undertaken to restore the sisters to liberty, and tells them to continue their usual labor until a suitable opportunity appears.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Isfendiyr / Isfendiyr is ordered to bring Rustem bound to the king, while Rustem and Isfendiyr negotiate guesthood, food, drink, and obedience. Rustem ultimately praises Isfendiyr after consulting his father Zl.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An opening speech expresses a preference for remaining free from crime and sequestered rather than aspiring to reign.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gushtsp tells Isfendiyr that he is his successor and that the crown and throne are his, then orders him to march to the scene of action.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Jamsp advises that a father's commands must be obeyed, and Isfendiyr consents to undertake the expedition.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Kitabn warns Isfendiyr that the enterprise is hopeless and that Rustem cannot honorably be placed in bonds; Isfendiyr says he does not fear Rustem but must keep his pledged word.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Isfendiyr leaves the next morning with a large army and great treasure. A camel lies down and will not rise, is ordered killed, and is interpreted by the people as a bad omen; Isfendiyr continues.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Isfendiyr sends his eldest son Bahman to invite Rustem to receive him, and Rustem comes to welcome Isfendiyr on foot after dismounting from Rakush.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Isfendiyr demands that Rustem submit to being bound hand and foot and says that refusal will lead to They recount an earlier succession in which Lohursp received the crown with Rustem's support, while Rustem offers to make Isfendiyr king. The two warriors agree to meet in battle, although Rustem fears the dishonor of killing a royal relative and suspects Gushtsp of treachery. Isfendiyr remains determined to fetter Rustem, who finally mounts his horse and leaves.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kai-khosru gave the regal crown to Lohursp, although the warriors considered Frburz, Ks's son, fitter by birth to rule.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rustem states that he and his father supported Lohursp, enabling Lohursp to sit on the throne.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Isfendiyr grasps and tightly wrings Rustem's hand, then proposes drinking that day and fighting with battle-axe and sword the next day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem says he would take Isfendiyr to Zl, place Bahman then orders the people of Sistan to be killed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Bashtan argues that the innocent people should not be killed; Bahman abandons the massacre, frees Zāl, restores Sistan to him, and returns to Persia.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the eighth year of his reign, Bahman is bitten by a snake and dies after remedies fail.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Bahman gives the crown and throne to his wife Huma, declaring that a future son of Huma will succeed him, while Huma will continue to reign if she has a daughter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The poem states that Fermurz's death occurs because Fate or Heaven has decreed it, despite his skill and effort.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Bahman","description":"King, grandson of Gushtsp, who conditions.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Zāl","description":"An old man and member of Rustem's family who pleads with Sistan.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"A figure whose alleged responsibility for Isfendiyr's death is used by reward.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Firdusi warns Mahmud that earthly power is temporary and urges him to fear God and refrain from
